nodes.name: approximate degree
nodes.statement: The approximate degree of a Boolean function $f \colon \{-1, 1\}^n \to \{-1, 1\}$, denoted $\adeg(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p$ such that $|p(x)-f(x)| \leq 1/3$ for all $x \in \bits^n$.
nodes.genus: the least degree of a real polynomial $p$

nodes.name: Beals et al. approximate degree lower bound on quantum query complexity
nodes.statement: In 1998, Beals et al.~\cite{beals} observed that the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$.
nodes.origin_citation: Beals et al., FOCS 1998 and J. ACM 2001
conclusions: the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$

nodes.name: polynomial method
nodes.statement: This method of proving quantum query lower bounds is called the \emph{polynomial method}.

nodes.name: frequency of a range item
nodes.statement: We let the \emph{frequency} $f_i$ of range item $i \in R$ denote the number of times $i$ appears in the input list.
nodes.genus: the number of times $i$ appears in the input list

nodes.name: Surjectivity ($\SURJ$)
nodes.statement: Surjectivity ($\SURJ$): Do all range items appear at least once?
nodes.origin_citation: Beame and Machmouchi, QIC 2012; Sherstov, FOCS 2015

nodes.name: $k$-distinctness
nodes.statement: $k$-distinctness: Is there a range item that appears $k$ or more times?

nodes.name: Image Size Testing
nodes.statement: Image Size Testing: Decide if all range items appear at least once or if at most $\gamma \cdot R$ range items appear at least once, under the promise that one of these is true.
nodes.origin_citation: Ambainis, Belovs, Regev, and de Wolf, SODA 2016

nodes.name: Statistical distance from uniform ($\SDU$)
nodes.statement: Statistical distance from uniform ($\SDU$): Interpret the input as a probability distribution $p$, where $p_i = f_i/N$. Compute the statistical distance of $p$ from the uniform distribution over $R$ up to some small additive error $\eps$.

nodes.name: Shannon entropy approximation
nodes.statement: Shannon entropy: Interpret the input as a probability distribution $p$, where $p_i = f_i/N$. Compute the Shannon entropy $\sum_{i \in R} p_i \cdot \log(1/p_i)$ of $p$ up to additive error $\eps$.

nodes.name: $k$-junta testing
nodes.statement: $k$-junta testing: Given an input in $\bits^n$ representing the truth table of a function $\bits^{\log n} \to \bits$, determine whether this function depends on at most $k$ of its input bits, or is at least $\eps$-far from any such function.
nodes.origin_citation: Ambainis et al., SODA 2016; Atıcı and Servedio

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: approximate degree of $\SURJ$
nodes.statement: The approximate degree of $\SURJ$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$.
assumptions: In the Surjectivity problem we are given $N$ numbers from $[R]$ and must decide if every range item appears at least once in the input.

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness
nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 2$, the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$.
conclusions: the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: Image Size Testing lower bound
nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
assumptions: In this problem, we are given $N$ numbers in $[R]$ and $0<\gamma<1$, and must decide if every range item appears at least once or if at most $\gamma\cdot R$ range items appear at least once.
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: $k$-junta testing lower bound
nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$.
assumptions: In this problem, we are given the truth table of a Boolean function and have to determine if the function depends on at most $k$ variables or if it is $\epsilon$-far from any such function.
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$.

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: $\SDU$ lower bound
nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution of a distribution over a range of size $n$ from the uniform distribution over the same range to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution of a distribution over a range of size $n$ from the uniform distribution over the same range to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$

nodes.name: Informal Theorem: Shannon entropy approximation lower bound
nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy of a distribution over a range of size $n$ to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy of a distribution over a range of size $n$ to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$

nodes.name: Grover-search algorithm for the special case of image size testing
nodes.statement: The version we define is solvable via the following simple algorithm making $O(\sqrt{n})$ queries: pick a random range item, and Grover search for an instance of that range item.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a random range item and Grover-search for an occurrence of it, using $O(\sqrt{n})$ queries.
output: must decide if every range item appears at least once or if at most $\gamma\cdot R$ range items appear at least once

nodes.name: dual polynomial (method of dual polynomials)
nodes.statement: To prove a lower bound for a function $f$ via this method, one exhibits an explicit \emph{dual polynomial} for $f$, which is a dual solution to a certain linear program capturing the approximate degree of $f$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
nodes.genus: a dual solution to a certain linear program

nodes.name: block-composition
nodes.statement: Here, a function $g \colon \bits^{n \cdot m} \to \bits$ is the block-composition of $h \colon \bits^n \to \bits$ and $f \colon \bits^m \to \bits$ if $g$ interprets its input as a sequence of $n$ blocks, applies $f$ to each block, and then feeds the $n$ outputs into $h$.

differentia: $g$ interprets its input as a sequence of $n$ blocks, applies $f$ to each block, and then feeds the $n$ outputs into $h$

nodes.name: Exhibit an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n)$
nodes.statement: One prominent example with many applications is to exhibit an AC$^0$ circuit over $n$ variables with approximate degree $\Omega(n)$.

nodes.name: Bun and Thaler: AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$
nodes.statement: For any constant $\delta \!>\! 0$, there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
conclusions: there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$

nodes.name: Sherstov: robustness / multiplicativity of approximate degree under composition
nodes.statement: For any Boolean functions $f$ and $h$, $\adeg(h \circ f) = O\left(\adeg(h) \cdot \adeg(f)\right)$.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: Every range item has frequency at most $T$, for a specific threshold $T=O(N^{1/3}) \ll N$.

nodes.name: Overview of the multi-phase construction of the approximation for $\mathsf{SURJ}$
nodes.statement: This suggested that an optimal approximation for $\mathsf{SURJ}$ should treat inputs satisfying \Cref{cond} differently than other inputs, leading us to the following multi-phase construction (for clarity and brevity, this overview is simplified). The first phase constructs a polynomial $p$ of degree $O(n^{3/4})$ approximating $\mathsf{SURJ}$ on all inputs satisfying \Cref{cond}. However, $p$ may be \emph{exponentially large} on other inputs. The second phase constructs a polynomial $q$ of degree $O(n^{3/4})$ that is \emph{exponentially small} on inputs $x$ that do \emph{not} satisfy \Cref{cond} (in particular, $q(x) \ll 1/p(x)$ for such $x$), and is close to 1 otherwise. The product $p \cdot q$ still approximates $\mathsf{SURJ}$ on inputs satisfying \Cref{cond}, and is \emph{exponentially small} on all other inputs. Notice that $\deg(p \cdot q) \leq \deg(p) + \deg(q) = O(n^{3/4})$. Combining the above with an additional averaging step (the details of which we omit from this introduction) yields an approximation to $\mathsf{SURJ}$ that is accurate on \emph{all} inputs.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply a degree-$O(n^{3/4})$ approximation valid on low-frequency inputs by a polynomial that is exponentially small elsewhere, then average.

nodes.name: dual polynomial witnessing $\adeg_\eps(f_n) \geq d$
nodes.statement: A dual polynomial that witnesses the fact that $\adeg_{\eps}(f_n) \geq d$ is a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \bits$ satisfying three properties: \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{x \in \bits^n}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \eps$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to be \emph{well-correlated} with $f$. \item $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} |\psi(x)| = 1$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to have $\ell_1$-norm equal to 1. \item For all polynomials $p \colon \bits^n \to \R$ of degree less than $d$, we have $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to have \emph{pure high degree} at least $d$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A dual witness for $\adeg_\eps(f)\ge d$ is well-correlated with $f$, has $\ell_1$-norm 1, and has pure high degree at least $d$.
differentia: For all polynomials $p \colon \bits^n \to \R$ of degree less than $d$, we have $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0$

nodes.name: Hamming weight decay condition
nodes.statement: Key to this step is the fact that the ``inner'' dual witness $\gamma$ for the high approximate degree of the $\OR_N$ function satisfies a ``Hamming weight decay'' condition: \begin{equation} |\gamma(x)| \cdot \binom{N}{|x|}\leq \frac{1}{\poly(|x|)},\end{equation} for a suitable polynomial function.

nodes.name: Exponentially stronger decay of the inner dual witness $\gamma$
nodes.statement: To improve the lower bound for $\SURJ$ from $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{2/3})$ to the optimal $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4})$, we observe that $\gamma$ in fact satisfies a much stronger decay condition: while the inverse-polynomial decay property of Equation \eqref{decaykey} is tight for small Hamming weights $|x|$, $|\gamma(x)|$ actually decays \emph{exponentially quickly} once $|x|$ is larger than a certain threshold $t$. This observation is enough to obtain the tight $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4})$ lower bound for $\SURJ$.
nodes.statement_short: $|\gamma(x)|$ decays exponentially, not just inverse-polynomially, past a threshold Hamming weight, which yields the tight $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4})$ bound.
assumptions: the inverse-polynomial decay property of Equation \eqref{decaykey} is tight for small Hamming weights $|x|$
conclusions: $|\gamma(x)|$ actually decays \emph{exponentially quickly} once $|x|$ is larger than a certain threshold $t$

nodes.name: $H^n_{\leq T}$ (low Hamming weight inputs)
nodes.statement: For $1 \le T \le n$, let $H^n_{\leq T}$ denote the subset of $\bits^n$ consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$. We use $|x|$ to denote the Hamming weight of an input $x \in \bits^n$, so $H^n_{\leq T} = \{x \in \bits^n \colon |x| \leq T\}$.
differentia: consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$

nodes.name: Approximate Degree With Boundedness Outside of the Promise Required
nodes.statement: Let $\eps > 0$ and $\cX \subseteq \bits^n$. The $\eps$-\emph{approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \cX \to \bits$, denoted $\adeg_\eps(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \cX \to \R$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \eps$ for all $x \in \cX$ and $|p(x)| \le 1 + \eps$ for all $x \in \bits^n \setminus \cX$. We use the term \emph{approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\adeg(f) = \adeg_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.statement_short: $\adeg_\eps(f)$ is the least degree of a polynomial approximating $f$ to error $\eps$ on the promise set that also stays bounded off it.
nodes.genus: the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \cX \to \R$

nodes.name: Dual formulation of approximate degree
nodes.statement: Let $\genericdomain \subseteq \bits^n$, and let $f : \genericdomain \to \{-1,1\}$. Then $\adeg_{\eps}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \R$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in \genericdomain}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) - \sum_{x \in \bits^n \setminus \genericdomain} |\psi(x)| > \eps, \\ &\sum_{x \in \bits^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \bits^n \to \R \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.origin_citation: Bun and Thaler, Theory of Computing
nodes.statement_short: LP duality: $\adeg_\eps(f)\ge d$ iff a unit-$\ell_1$-norm dual witness of pure high degree $d$ correlates with $f$ better than $\eps$.
conclusions: $\adeg_{\eps}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \R$ satisfying the following properties
For every polynomial $p \colon \bits^n \to \R$ of degree less than $d$, $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0$

nodes.name: dual polynomials, $\ell_1$-norm, pure high degree
nodes.statement: We will refer to functions $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \reals$ as \emph{dual polynomials}. We refer to $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} |\psi(x)|$ as the $\ell_1$-norm of $\psi$, and denote this quantity by $\|\psi\|_1$. If $\psi$ satisfies Equation \eqref{eq:phd}, it is said to have \emph{pure high degree} at least $d$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.name: correlation $\langle f, \psi \rangle$
nodes.statement: Given a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \R$, and a (possibly partial) function $f \colon \genericdomain \to \bits$, where $\genericdomain \subseteq \bits^n$, we let $\langle f, \psi \rangle := \sum_{x \in \genericdomain} f(x) \cdot \psi(x) - \sum_{x \in \bits^n \setminus \genericdomain} |\psi(x)|$, and refer to this as the correlation of $f$ and $\psi$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.name: Approximate Degree With Unboundedness Permitted Outside of the Promise
nodes.statement: Let $\eps > 0$ and $\cX$ be a finite set. The $\eps$-\emph{unbounded approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \cX \to \bits$, denoted $\ubdeg_\eps(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \cX \to \R$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \eps$ for all $x \in \cX$ (if $\cX$ is a strict subset of a larger domain, then no constraints are placed on $p(x)$ for $x \not\in \cX$). We use the term \emph{unbounded approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\ubdeg(f) = \ubdeg_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.statement_short: $\ubdeg_\eps(f)$ is the least degree of a polynomial approximating $f$ on the promise set, with no constraint outside it.
nodes.genus: the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \cX \to \R$
differentia: if $\cX$ is a strict subset of a larger domain, then no constraints are placed on $p(x)$ for $x \not\in \cX$

nodes.name: Dual formulation of unbounded approximate degree
nodes.statement: Let $\genericdomain \subseteq \bits^n$, and let $f : \genericdomain \to \{-1,1\}$. Then $\ubdeg_{\eps}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \R$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\psi(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in \genericdomain, \\ &\sum_{x \in \genericdomain}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \eps, \\ &\sum_{x \in \bits^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \bits^n \to \R \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: Same as the bounded dual characterization, but the witness must vanish outside the promise set.
conclusions: $\ubdeg_{\eps}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \bits^n \to \R$ satisfying the following properties
For every polynomial $p \colon \bits^n \to \R$ of degree less than $d$, $\sum_{x \in \bits^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0$

nodes.name: Nisan-Szegedy bounds for $\AND$ and $\OR$
nodes.statement: For any constant $\eps \in (0, 1)$, the functions $\AND$ and $\OR$ on $n$ bits have $\eps$-approximate degree $\Theta(n^{1/2})$, and the same holds for their negations.
conclusions: the functions $\AND$ and $\OR$ on $n$ bits have $\eps$-approximate degree $\Theta(n^{1/2})$
the same holds for their negations

nodes.name: Minsky-Papert symmetrization
nodes.statement: Let $p \colon \bits^n \to \bits$ be an arbitrary polynomial and let $[n]_0$ denote the set $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$. Then there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \R \to \R$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$ such that \[q(t) = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{ t}} \sum_{x \in \bits^n \colon |x|=t} p(x)\] for all $t \in [n]_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Averaging a polynomial over each Hamming layer yields a univariate polynomial of no larger degree.
conclusions: there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \R \to \R$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$ such that $q(t) = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{ t}} \sum_{x \in \bits^n \colon |x|=t} p(x)$ for all $t \in [n]_0$

nodes.name: $\SURJ_{N, R}$ (Surjectivity)
nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\SURJ_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \bits$ by $\SURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
differentia: $\SURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$

nodes.name: $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$ (Surjectivity with a dummy item)
nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\dumSURJ_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \bits$ by $\dumSURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
differentia: $\dumSURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$

nodes.name: Reduction from $\dumSURJ$ to $\SURJ$
nodes.statement: Let $\eps > 0$ and $N \ge R$. Then \[ \adeg_\eps(\dumSURJ_{N, R}) \le \adeg_\eps(\SURJ_{N + 1, R + 1}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]

nodes.name: Proof of the $\dumSURJ$-to-$\SURJ$ reduction
nodes.statement: Let $p : \bits^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \bits$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\SURJ_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$. Recall that an input to $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$. Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\dumSURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \SURJ_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Map the dummy item $0$ to the extra range element $R+1$ by a degree-$\log(R+1)$ transformation and substitute into the approximation for $\SURJ_{N+1,R+1}$.

nodes.name: Take an approximation for $\SURJ_{N+1,R+1}$
nodes.statement: Let $p : \bits^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \bits$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\SURJ_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a degree-$d$ approximation to the larger Surjectivity instance.

nodes.name: Define the transformation $T$
nodes.statement: Recall that an input to $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$. Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the map sending the dummy item $0$ to the new range element $R+1$.

nodes.name: Bound the degree of $T$ and verify the identity
nodes.statement: Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\dumSURJ_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \SURJ_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\]
nodes.statement_short: $T$ has degree $\log(R+1)$ and realizes $\dumSURJ$ as a restriction of $\SURJ$.

nodes.name: Conclude the degree bound
nodes.statement: Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Composition gives a degree-$d\log(R+1)$ approximation to $\dumSURJ_{N,R}$.

nodes.name: $\DIST^k_{N, R}$ ($k$-distinctness)
nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\DIST^k_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \bits$ by $\DIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.
differentia: $\DIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$

nodes.name: $\dumDIST^k_{N, R}$ ($k$-distinctness with a dummy item)
nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\dumDIST^k_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \bits$ by $\dumDIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.
differentia: $\dumDIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$

nodes.name: Why the restriction $k \ge 2$ is essential
nodes.statement: For $k \ge 2$, a lower bound on the approximate degree of $\dumDIST^k$ implies a lower bound on the approximate degree of $\DIST^k$. The restriction that $k \ge 2$ is essential, because the function $\DIST^1$ is the constant function that evaluates to $\mathsf{TRUE}$ on \emph{any} input (since at least one range item must always have frequency at least one), whereas $\dumDIST^1$ contains $\OR_N$ as a subfunction, and hence has approximate degree at least $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$.
nodes.statement_short: $\DIST^1$ is constant while $\dumDIST^1$ contains $\OR_N$, so the dummy-item reduction needs $k\ge 2$.

nodes.name: Reduction from $\dumDIST^k$ to $\DIST^k$
nodes.statement: Let $\eps > 0$, $N, R \in \N$, and $k \ge 2$. Then \[ \deg_\eps(\dumDIST^k_{N, R}) \le \deg_\eps(\DIST^k_{N, R+N}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]

nodes.name: Proof of the $\dumDIST^k$-to-$\DIST^k$ reduction
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}, but uses a slightly more involved reduction. Let $p : \bits^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \bits$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\DIST^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumDIST^k_{N, R}$. For each $i = 1, \dots, R$, define a transformation $T_i : [R]_0 \to [R+N]$ by \[T_i(s) = \begin{cases} R + i & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] As a mapping between binary representations, the function $T=(T_1, \dots, T_N)$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\dumDIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \DIST^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$.

nodes.name: Take an approximation for $\DIST^k_{N,R+N}$

Let $p : \bits^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \bits$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\DIST^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumDIST^k_{N, R}$.

nodes.name: Verify the identity and conclude
nodes.statement: For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\dumDIST^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \DIST^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\eps$-approximates $\dumSURJ_{N, R}$.

nodes.name: block composition
nodes.statement: For functions $f : Y^n \to Z$ and $g: X \to Y$, define the \emph{block composition} $f \circ g : X^n \to Z$ by $(f\circ g)(x_1, \dots, x_n) = f(g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n))$, for all $x_1, \dots, x_n \in X$.

nodes.name: symmetric function
nodes.statement: Suppose $g$ is a \emph{symmetric} function, in the sense that for any $x \in \bits^N$ and any permutation $\sigma : [N] \to [N]$, we have \[g(x_1, \dots, x_N) = g(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(N)}).\] Equivalently, the value of $g$ on any input $x$ depends only on its Hamming weight $|x|$.

nodes.name: $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ and $F^{\le N}$
nodes.statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ give rise to two functions. The first, which we denote by $F^{\operatorname{prop}} : [R]_0^N \to \bits$, is a certain property of a list of numbers $s_1, \dots, s_N \in [R]_0$. The second, which we denote by $F^{\le N} : H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R} \to \bits$, is the block composition of $f$ and $g$ restricted to inputs of Hamming weight at most $N$. Formally, these functions are defined as: \begin{align*} &F^{\operatorname{prop}}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = f(g(\id[s_1 = 1], \dots, \id[s_N = 1]), \dots, g(\id[s_1=R], \dots,\id[s_N=R])) \\ &F^{\le N}(x_1, \dots, x_R) = \begin{cases} f(g(x_1), \dots, g(x_R)) & \text{ if } x_1, \dots, x_R \in \bits^N, |x_1| + \dots + |x_R| \le N.\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ is the list property induced by $f\circ g$; $F^{\le N}$ is the block composition restricted to Hamming weight $\le N$.

nodes.name: Bun-Thaler reduction between symmetric properties and block compositions
nodes.statement: Let $f : \bits^R \to \bits$ be any function and let $g : \bits^N \to \bits$ be a symmetric function. Then for $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ and $F^{\le N}$ defined above, and for any $\eps > 0$, we have \[\deg_\eps(F^{\operatorname{prop}}) \ge \ubdeg_\eps(F^{\le N}).\]

nodes.name: Reduction for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Let $N, R \in \N$. Then for any $\eps > 0$, \[\adeg_\eps(\dumSURJ_{N, R}) \ge \ubdeg_\eps(F^{\le N})\] where $F^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \bits$ is the restriction of $\AND_R \circ \OR_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$.

assumptions: $F^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \bits$ is the restriction of $\AND_R \circ \OR_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$

nodes.name: $\THR^k_N$ (threshold function)
nodes.statement: For integers $k, N$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\THR^k_N : \bits^N \to \bits$ by $\THR^k_N(x) = -1$ iff $|x| \ge k$.

nodes.name: Reduction for $k$-distinctness
nodes.statement: Let $N, R \in \N$. Then for any $\eps > 0$, \[\adeg_\eps(\dumDIST^k_{N, R}) \ge \ubdeg_\eps(G^{\le N})\] where $G^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \bits$ is the restriction of $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$.

nodes.name: dual block composition
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi : \bits^M \to \R$ and $\psi : \bits^m \to \R$ be functions that are not identically zero. Let $x=(x_1, \dots, x_M) \in \left(\bits^{m}\right)^M$. Define the \emph{dual block composition} of $\Psi$ and $\psi$, denoted $\Psi \ls \psi : (\bits^m)^M \to \R$, by \[(\Psi \ls \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M) = 2^M \cdot \Psi(\dots, \sgn\left(\psi(x_i)\right), \dots) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^M |\psi(x_i)|.\]

nodes.name: Properties of the dual block composition
nodes.statement: The dual block composition satisfies the following properties: \paragraph{\emph{Preservation of $\ell_1$-norm}:} If $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$, $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$, and $\langle \psi, \mathbf{1}\rangle = 0$, then \begin{equation}\|\Psi \ls \psi\|_1 = 1. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Multiplicativity of pure high degree}:} If $\langle \Psi, P \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $P \colon \bits^M \to \bits$ of degree less than $D$, and $\langle \psi, p \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $p \colon \bits^m \to \bits$ of degree less than $d$, then for every polynomial $q \colon \bits^{m \cdot M} \to \bits$, \begin{equation}\deg q < D \cdot d \implies \langle \Psi \ls \psi, q \rangle = 0. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Associativity}:} For every $\zeta: \bits^{m_\zeta} \to \R$, $\varphi: \bits^{m_\varphi} \to \R$, and $\psi: \bits^{m_\psi} \to \R$, we have \begin{equation} (\zeta \ls \varphi) \ls \psi = \zeta \ls (\varphi \ls \psi). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Dual block composition preserves unit $\ell_1$-norm, multiplies pure high degrees, and is associative.
assumptions: If $\langle \Psi, P \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $P \colon \bits^M \to \bits$ of degree less than $D$, and $\langle \psi, p \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $p \colon \bits^m \to \bits$ of degree less than $d$

nodes.name: $(\alpha, \beta)$-decay condition
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \N$ and $\alpha, \beta > 0$. A function $\omega: [M]_0 \to \R$ satisfies the $(\alpha, \beta)$-decay condition if \begin{align} &\sum_{t = 0}^M \omega(t) = 0, \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^M |\omega(t)| = 1, \\ &|\omega(t)| \le \alpha \exp (-\beta t) / t^2 \quad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, M. \end{align}

nodes.name: Zeroing out high Hamming weight mass (refinement of Bun-Thaler)

nodes.name: The key refinement of the zeroing-out proposition
nodes.statement: The key refinement of \Cref{prop:btzeroing} relative to the analysis of Bun and Thaler is that \Cref{prop:btzeroing} applies when $N=\Theta(R)$ (assuming $\alpha=O(1))$. In contrast, the techniques of Bun and Thaler required $N=\Omega(R \cdot \log^2 R)$. As indicated in \Cref{s:overviewoftheproofs}, this refinement will be essential in obtaining our lower bounds for $\SDU$, entropy approximation, and junta testing for constant proximity parameter.

nodes.name: Two-step structure of the proof of the zeroing-out proposition
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{prop:btzeroing} occurs in two steps. First, in \Cref{prop:prelim-mass}, we show that $\xi = \Phi \ls \psi$ places an exponentially small amount of mass on inputs outside of $H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}$. Second, in \Cref{prop:correction}, we construct a correction object $\nu$ that zeroes out the mass $\xi$ places outside of $H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}$ without decreasing its pure high degree. Combining $\xi$ with $\nu$ yields the desired object $\zeta$.

nodes.name: Proof of the combinatorial lemma
nodes.statement: Let $T = \lfloor \frac{N}{2M} \rfloor$. For each $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$, let \[C(s) = \max \left\{ \frac{N}{6 s \ln R}, \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R \cdot s}} \right\}.\] We begin with a simple, but important, structural observation about the set $P$. Let $t = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R$ be a sequence such that $t_1 + \dots + t_R > N$. Then we claim that there exists an $s \in \{T \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \ge C(s)$ for at least $s$ indices $i \in [R]$. To see this, assume without loss of generality that the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted so that $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_R$. Then there must exist an $s \geq T$ such that $t_s \ge C(s)$. Otherwise, because no $t_i$ can exceed $M$, we would have: \begin{align*} t_1 + \dots + t_R &< T \cdot M + \sum_{s = 1}^R C(s) \\ &\le \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{6 \ln R} \sum_{s = 1}^{\lfloor R / \ln^2 R \rfloor} \frac{1}{s} + \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R}} \sum_{s = \lceil R / \ln^2 R \rceil}^R \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}\\ &\le \frac{N}{2}+ \frac{N}{6} + \frac{N}{3} \\ &= N. \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \Cref{lem:inv-sqrt} and the fact that $\sum_{s = 1}^m s^{-1} \le \ln m + 1$ (and $R$ is sufficiently large). Since the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted, the preceding values $t_1, \dots, t_{s-1} \geq C(s)$ as well. For each subset $S \subseteq [R]$, define \[P_S = \{\vec{t} \in P : t_i \ge C(|S|)\text{ for all indices }i \in S\}.\] The observations above guarantee that for every $\vec{t}=(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P$, there exists some set $S$ of size at least $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \geq C(s)$ for all $i \in S$. Hence \begin{align*} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \sum_{S \subseteq [R] : |S| = s} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P_S} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \\ & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r=\lceil C(s) \rceil}^M \eta_i(r)\right) \right)^s \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \right)\right)^{R-s} & \\ &\leq 2^{-R}\sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^M 2\alpha \exp(-\beta r ) r^{-2} \right)^s & \text{by Properties } \eqref{eqn:eta-bound} \text{ and } \eqref{eqn:eta-decay}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^\infty \exp\left(-\beta r s\right) & \text{by \Cref{lem:binomial}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \cdot \exp\left(-\beta s C(s)\right) & \text{by \Cref{lem:inv-exp-tail}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{72\alpha R s}{N^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta N}{6\ln R}\right) & \text{by definition of $C(s)$}\\ &\qquad\qquad\text{ and since } \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \le \frac{1}{1 - (1-\beta/2)} = \frac{2}{\beta} \text{ for } s \ge 1, \beta \in (0, 1) & \\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} 2^{-s} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{3 \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R }{ \ln R} + \ln(2/\beta)\right)& \text{setting } N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R \\ &\le 2^{-R} \cdot (2 N R)^{-2\Delta}, \end{align*} where \[\Delta = \frac{1}{2\ln(2NR)} \cdot \left(\frac{3\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{\ln R} - \ln(2/\beta) \right) \ge \frac{\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{4\ln^2 R}\] holds for sufficiently large $R$ by the restrictions placed on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the statement of the lemma.
