nodes.name: Upper bound on the approximate degree of Surjectivity
nodes.statement: For any $R \in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\adeg(\SURJ_{N,R}) = \tO(N^{3/4})$.

nodes.name: Reduction of the upper bound to the case $R=\Theta(N)$
nodes.statement: For the remainder of the section, we focus on proving \Cref{thm:upper} in the case that $R=\Theta(N)$. This is without loss of generality by the following argument. If $R > N$, then \Surjectivity\ is identically false, and hence has (exact) degree 0. And if $R=o(N)$, then we can reduce to the case $R=\Theta(N)$ as follows. Let $N'=2N$ and $R' = R + N$; clearly $R' = \Theta(N)$. Given an input $x$ to $\SURJ_{N, R}$, obtain an input $x'$ to $\SURJ_{N', R'}$ by appending range elements $R+1, \dots, R+N$ to $x$. This construction guarantees that $\SURJ_{N, R}(x) = \SURJ_{N', R'}(x')$. It follows that an approximation of degree $\tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$ for $\SURJ_{N', R'}$ implies an approximation of the same degree for $\SURJ_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis: $R>N$ makes $\SURJ$ constant, and $R=o(N)$ reduces to $R=\Theta(N)$ by padding the input with fresh range elements.

nodes.name: Case $R > N$
nodes.statement: If $R > N$, then \Surjectivity\ is identically false, and hence has (exact) degree 0.
nodes.statement_short: When the range is larger than the list, $\SURJ$ is constant.

nodes.name: Case $R = o(N)$: pad the input
nodes.statement: And if $R=o(N)$, then we can reduce to the case $R=\Theta(N)$ as follows. Let $N'=2N$ and $R' = R + N$; clearly $R' = \Theta(N)$. Given an input $x$ to $\SURJ_{N, R}$, obtain an input $x'$ to $\SURJ_{N', R'}$ by appending range elements $R+1, \dots, R+N$ to $x$. This construction guarantees that $\SURJ_{N, R}(x) = \SURJ_{N', R'}(x')$. It follows that an approximation of degree $\tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$ for $\SURJ_{N', R'}$ implies an approximation of the same degree for $\SURJ_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Padding with $N$ new range items reduces to the balanced case.

nodes.name: $\eps$-approximating polynomial in the $\{0,1\}$ convention
nodes.statement: First, we will consider Boolean functions $f : \B^n \to \B$, where $1$ corresponds to logical $\mathsf{TRUE}$ and $0$ corresponds to logical $\mathsf{FALSE}$. For such a Boolean function, we say that a polynomial $p : \B^n \to \R$ is an $\eps$-approximating polynomial for $f$ if $p(x) \in [0, \eps]$ when $f(x) = 0$ and $p(x) \in [1-\eps, 1]$ when $f(x) = 1$.

nodes.name: Warmup example: approximating $\NOR$
nodes.statement: To convey the intuition behind our polynomial construction for \Surjectivity, we start by considering a much simpler function as an illustrative example. Consider the negation of the $\OR$ function on $n$ bits, $\NOR \colon \B^n\to\B$. We will give a novel construction of an approximating polynomial for $\NOR$ of degree $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Of course, this is not terribly interesting since it is already known that $\adeg(\NOR) = \Theta(\sqrt{n})$ (cf. \Cref{andornor}). But this construction highlights the main idea behind the more involved constructions to follow.
nodes.statement_short: $\NOR$ serves as a warmup: a new $\tilde{O}(\sqrt n)$-degree construction that previews the two-polynomial product trick.

nodes.name: the hard set $\P$ for $\NOR$
nodes.statement: Let us refer to the set of low-Hamming weight inputs as $\P$, i.e., \begin{equation} \P = H^n_{\le T} = \{x\in\B^n: 0\leq |x| \leq T\}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the set of low-Hamming weight inputs

nodes.name: An informal description of the polynomial approximation for $\NOR$
nodes.statement: \State Using $q$, check if $|x|>T$ (with exponentially small probability of error if indeed $|x| > T$). If so, halt and output 0. \State Using $p$, compute $\NOR$ under the promise that $0\leq |x| \leq T$ and output the result.
nodes.statement_short: First screen out high Hamming weight inputs with $q$, then evaluate $\NOR$ on the low-weight promise with $p$.

nodes.name: Screen out high Hamming weight inputs
nodes.statement: \State Using $q$, check if $|x|>T$ (with exponentially small probability of error if indeed $|x| > T$). If so, halt and output 0.
nodes.statement_short: Reject inputs of Hamming weight above $T$ using $q$.

nodes.name: Evaluate $\NOR$ under the low-weight promise
nodes.statement: \State Using $p$, compute $\NOR$ under the promise that $0\leq |x| \leq T$ and output the result.
nodes.statement_short: Return $p$'s value, which is accurate when $|x|\le T$.

nodes.name: polynomials as algorithms (informal terminology)
nodes.statement: Consider three Boolean functions $p_1:\B^n\to\B$, $p_2:\B^n\to\B$ and $p_3:\B^n\to\B$, and suppose there are deterministic algorithms $A_1$, $A_2$, and $A_3$ that compute these Boolean functions exactly. Now it makes sense to say ``run algorithm $A_1$ in input $x$; if it accepts then output $A_2(x)$, and if it rejects, then output $A_3(x)$.'' The Boolean function computed by this is $A_2(x)$ if $A_1(x)=1$ and $A_3(x)$ if $A_1(x)=0$. Observe that the following polynomial composition of $p_1, p_2, p_3$ computes the same Boolean function: $p_1(x)p_2(x) + (1-p_1(x))p_3(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Branching on $p_1$ and then running $p_2$ or $p_3$ corresponds to the polynomial $p_1p_2 + (1-p_1)p_3$.

nodes.name: Properties of Chebyshev Polynomials
nodes.statement: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item There exists a polynomial $T_d : \R \to \R$ (the Chebyshev polynomial of degree $d$) such that $T_d(x) \in [-1, 1]$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$ and $T_d(1 + \mu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \exp(d\sqrt{\mu})$ for all $\mu \in (0, 1)$. \item For any polynomial $p : \R \to \R$ of degree $d$ with $|p(x)| \le 1$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$, we have that for any $x$ with $|x| > 1$, \begin{equation} |p(x)| \leq |T_d(x)| \leq (2|x|)^d, \end{equation} where $T_d$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of degree $d$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev polynomials are bounded on $[-1,1]$, grow like $\exp(d\sqrt\mu)$ just outside it, and dominate any such bounded polynomial.
assumptions: For any polynomial $p : \R \to \R$ of degree $d$ with $|p(x)| \le 1$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$
conclusions: There exists a polynomial $T_d : \R \to \R$ (the Chebyshev polynomial of degree $d$) such that $T_d(x) \in [-1, 1]$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$ and $T_d(1 + \mu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \exp(d\sqrt{\mu})$ for all $\mu \in (0, 1)$

nodes.name: Proof of the Chebyshev polynomial properties
nodes.statement: To establish property (1), we use the fact that for $\mu > 0$, the value of the degree $d$ Chebyshev polynomial can be written~\cite[\S 3.2 Problem 8(f)]{cheney} as \begin{align*} T_d(1 + \mu) &= \cosh ( d \operatorname{arcosh} ( 1 + \mu) ) \\ & \ge \cosh ( d \sqrt{\mu} ) & \text{ for } \mu \le 1\\ & \ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \exp(d \sqrt{\mu}). \end{align*} Property (2) appears as~\cite[3.2 Problem 19]{cheney}.
nodes.statement_short: Property (1) follows from the $\cosh$ representation of $T_d$; property (2) is quoted from Cheney.

nodes.name: Establish property (1) via the $\cosh$ representation
nodes.statement: To establish property (1), we use the fact that for $\mu > 0$, the value of the degree $d$ Chebyshev polynomial can be written~\cite[\S 3.2 Problem 8(f)]{cheney} as \begin{align*} T_d(1 + \mu) &= \cosh ( d \operatorname{arcosh} ( 1 + \mu) ) \\ & \ge \cosh ( d \sqrt{\mu} ) & \text{ for } \mu \le 1\\ & \ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \exp(d \sqrt{\mu}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\cosh(d\,\mathrm{arcosh}(1+\mu))$ from below by $\frac12 e^{d\sqrt\mu}$.

nodes.name: Quote property (2)
nodes.statement: Property (2) appears as~\cite[3.2 Problem 19]{cheney}.
nodes.statement_short: Property (2) is a standard extremal property of Chebyshev polynomials.

nodes.name: Approximating $\OR$ on Inputs of Low Hamming Weight
nodes.statement: Let $\eps \in (0, 1)$ and $1 \le T \le N$. There is a polynomial $V_{T, \eps}:\B^N\to \R$ of degree $O(\sqrt{T}\log (1/\eps))$ such that \begin{align} V_{T, \eps}(x) \in \begin{cases} [0,\eps] &\mathrm{if}~ |x| = 0 \\ [1-\eps,1] & \mathrm{if}~ 1\leq |x| \leq T \\ [-a, a] \text{ for some } a \in {\exp\left(O\left(\sqrt{T} \cdot \log N \cdot \log\left(1/\eps\right)\right)\right)} & \mathrm{if}~ |x| > T \end{cases}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: There is a degree-$O(\sqrt T\log(1/\eps))$ polynomial approximating $\OR$ to error $\eps$ up to Hamming weight $T$, exponentially bounded beyond it.
conclusions: There is a polynomial $V_{T, \eps}:\B^N\to \R$ of degree $O(\sqrt{T}\log (1/\eps))$ such that $V_{T, \eps}(x) \in [0,\eps]$ if $|x| = 0$
$V_{T, \eps}(x) \in [-a, a]$ for some $a \in \exp\left(O\left(\sqrt{T} \cdot \log N \cdot \log\left(1/\eps\right)\right)\right)$ if $|x| > T$

nodes.name: Proof of the low-Hamming-weight $\OR$ approximation
nodes.statement: Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\eps))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\eps$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \eps}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$: \[V_{T, \eps}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\] Then for $|x| = 0$, we have \[V_{T, \eps}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\] If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \eps(x)} \in [1-\eps, 1]$. Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then \[|V_{T, \eps}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\eps)),\] where the final inequality holds by Equation \eqref{eq:swell}.
nodes.statement_short: Take an affine transformation of the Chebyshev polynomial $T_d$ scaled so that it is $0$ at weight $0$ and near $1$ up to weight $T$.

nodes.name: Choose the degree and define $V_{T,\eps}$
nodes.statement: Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\eps))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\eps$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \eps}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$: \[V_{T, \eps}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\]
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the Chebyshev polynomial so that its blowup at $1+1/T$ is at least $2/\eps$.

nodes.name: Verify the value at Hamming weight $0$
nodes.statement: Then for $|x| = 0$, we have \[V_{T, \eps}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\]
nodes.statement_short: The affine shift makes $V_{T,\eps}$ vanish on the all-zeros input.

nodes.name: Verify the range $1 \le |x| \le T$
nodes.statement: If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \eps(x)} \in [1-\eps, 1]$.
nodes.statement_short: On low nonzero weights the argument stays inside $[-1,1]$ where $T_d$ is bounded.

nodes.name: Bound the growth above weight $T$
nodes.statement: Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then \[|V_{T, \eps}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\eps)),\] where the final inequality holds by Equation \eqref{eq:swell}.
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev growth gives the exponential bound outside the promise.

nodes.name: Buhrman et al. block composition of approximating polynomials
nodes.statement: Let $f : \B^n \to \B$ and $g : X \to \B$ be Boolean functions, where $X \subseteq \{0, 1\}^m$ for some $m$. Let $p : \B^n \to [0, 1]$ be an $\eps$-approximating polynomial for $f$, and let $q : X \to [0, 1]$ be a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$. Then the block composition $p \circ q : X^n \to \R$ is an $(\eps + \delta n)$-approximating polynomial for $f \circ g : X^n \to \B$.
nodes.origin_citation: Buhrman, Newman, Röhrig, and de Wolf
assumptions: Let $f : \B^n \to \B$ and $g : X \to \B$ be Boolean functions, where $X \subseteq \{0, 1\}^m$ for some $m$
let $q : X \to [0, 1]$ be a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$
conclusions: the block composition $p \circ q : X^n \to \R$ is an $(\eps + \delta n)$-approximating polynomial for $f \circ g : X^n \to \B$

nodes.name: Proof of the naive composition lemma
nodes.statement: Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \B^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\eps$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$. Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\B^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have \[p(z) = \E[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \E[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\] Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$. Hence, \[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\] Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.
nodes.origin_citation: Buhrman, Newman, Röhrig, and de Wolf
nodes.statement_short: Interpret $z=q(x)$ as biases of a random Boolean string $Z$ and use multilinearity of $p$ plus a union bound on $\Pr[Z\ne y]$.

nodes.name: Reduce to bounding $|p(y)-p(z)|$
nodes.statement: Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \B^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\eps$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality reduces the claim to comparing $p$ at $y$ and at $z$.

nodes.name: Introduce the random string $Z$
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\B^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have \[p(z) = \E[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \E[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\]
nodes.statement_short: Multilinearity turns $p(z)$ into an expectation over a product distribution.

nodes.name: Bound $\Pr[Z=y]$
nodes.statement: Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$. Hence, \[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\]
nodes.statement_short: Each coordinate is correct with probability $1-\delta$, so all agree with probability $1-\delta n$.

nodes.name: Conclude the two-sided bound
nodes.statement: Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of $p$ in $[0,1]$ gives $|p(y)-p(z)|\le\delta n$.

nodes.name: $\fr_r(x)$, the multiplicity of range element $r$
nodes.statement: In this section, we will use the notation \begin{equation} \fr_r(x) = |\{i \in [N]: x_i=r\}| \end{equation} to denote the number of times the range element $r$ appears in the input $x$. Note that the \Surjectivity\ function evaluates to $1$ if and only if $\fr_r(x)\geq 1$ for all $r\in[R]$.
nodes.genus: the number of times the range element $r$ appears in the input $x$

nodes.name: $\Rcal$-Surjectivity $\SURJ_{\Rcal}$
nodes.statement: Finally, we will also need to consider a generalized version of \Surjectivity, $\Rcal$-\Surjectivity\ for some set $\Rcal \subseteq [R]$, which we denote $\SURJ_{\Rcal}$. As with \Surjectivity, \begin{equation} \SURJ_{\Rcal}:[R]^N \to \B, \end{equation} and $\SURJ_{\Rcal}(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = 1$ if and only if for all $r \in \Rcal$ there exists an $i\in [N]$ such that $x_i = r$. In other words, $\SURJ_\Rcal(x)=1$ if and only if for all $r\in\Rcal$ we have $\fr_r(x)\geq 1$. Note that $\SURJ_{[R]} = \SURJ$. Our construction will actually show more generally that $\adeg(\SURJ_{\Rcal}) = \tO(N^{3/4})$ for all $\Rcal \subseteq [R]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\SURJ_\Rcal$ asks whether every range item in the subset $\Rcal$ appears at least once.
differentia: $\SURJ_{\Rcal}(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = 1$ if and only if for all $r \in \Rcal$ there exists an $i\in [N]$ such that $x_i = r$

nodes.name: the hard input sets $\mathcal{P}$ and $\P_\Rcal$ for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: To this end, we define $\mathcal{P}$ as the set of inputs for which every range item appears at most $T$ times, for a parameter $T$ to be chosen later: \begin{equation} \mathcal{P}=\{x:\forall r\in [R],~\fr_r(x)\leq T\}. \end{equation} More generally, when we consider $\Rcal$-\Surjectivity, we denote the set of hard inputs $\P_\Rcal$ and define it as \begin{equation} \P_\Rcal=\{x:\forall r\in \Rcal,~\fr_r(x)\leq T\}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the set of inputs for which every range item appears at most $T$ times

nodes.name: $\SURJ_\Rcal$ as an $\AND$ of $\OR$s
nodes.statement: To construct a polynomial that works on the hard inputs, $\P_\Rcal$, we first express $\SURJ_\Rcal$ as \begin{equation} \SURJ_\Rcal(x) = \bigwedge_{r\in\Rcal} \bigvee_{i\in[N]} \id[x_i=r], \end{equation} where $\id[x_i=r]$ is the indicator function that takes value $1$ when $x_i=r$ and $0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: $p_{\mathcal{R}}$ approximates $\SURJ_{\Rcal}$ on the hard inputs
nodes.statement: $|p_{\mathcal{R}}(x) - \SURJ_{\Rcal}(x)| \leq 1/10$ for all $x \in \P_\Rcal$.

nodes.name: formal definition of $p_{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: Let $w$ be a $(1/20)$-approximating polynomial for $\AND_{|\mathcal{R}|}$ of degree $O(|\mathcal{R}|^{1/2})$ whose existence is guaranteed by \Cref{andornor}. We may assume that $w(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \B^n$ (we will exploit this assumption in the proof of \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ} below, as it allows us to apply \Cref{lem:real-bound} below to $w$). Let $q := w \circ V_{T, 1/(20n)}$. Finally, let us define $p_{\mathcal{R}}$ to be the composition of $q$ with the indicator functions $\{\id[x_i=r]\}_{i \in [N], r \in \mathcal{R}}$. For example, if $\mathcal{R}=\{1, \dots, |\mathcal{R}|\}$, then \begin{equation*} p_{\mathcal{R}} = q\left(\id\left[x_1 = 1\right], \id\left[x_2=1\right], \dots, \id\left[x_N=1\right], \id\left[x_1=2\right], \dots, \id\left[x_N=\left|\mathcal{R}\right|\right]\right). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $p_\Rcal$ is $w\circ V_{T,1/(20n)}$ composed with the equality indicators, where $w$ approximates $\AND_{|\Rcal|}$.
nodes.genus: the composition of $q$ with the indicator functions $\{\id[x_i=r]\}_{i \in [N], r \in \mathcal{R}}$

nodes.name: Degree bound for $p_{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: Observe that $$\deg(p_{\mathcal{R}}) \leq \deg(w) \cdot \deg(V_{T, 1/(20n)}) \cdot \deg(\id[x_i=r]) \leq O\left(|\mathcal{R}|^{1/2} \cdot T^{1/2} \log n \cdot \log R\right) \leq \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{NT}\right).$$

nodes.name: $b_\Rcal(x)$, the number of frequent range items
nodes.statement: For an input $x\in [R]^N$ outside of $\P_\Rcal$, let $b_\Rcal(x)$ be the number of range items that appear more than $T$ times, i.e., \begin{equation} b_\Rcal(x) = |\{r\in\Rcal:\fr_r(x)>T\}|. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the number of range items that appear more than $T$ times

nodes.name: Exponential bound on $p_{\mathcal{R}}$ outside the hard set
nodes.statement: We claim that $|p_{\mathcal{R}}(x) | \leq {\exp\left(b_\Rcal(x) \cdot \tO(\sqrt{T})\right)}$.

nodes.name: Growth bound for multilinear polynomials bounded on the cube
nodes.statement: Let $p : \R^n \to \R$ be a multilinear polynomial with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \B^n$. Then for $x \in \R^n$, we have \[|p(x)| \le \prod_{i = 1}^n (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|).\]
assumptions: Let $p : \R^n \to \R$ be a multilinear polynomial with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \B^n$

nodes.name: Proof of the multilinear growth bound
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true. Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \R^n \to \R$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \B^n$. We begin by decomposing \[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\] where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \B^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \B^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \B^{n-1}$. Now for any $x \in \R^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have \begin{align*} |p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\ &\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\ &\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|) \end{align*} where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $n$: split off the last variable and apply the inductive hypothesis to the two multilinear halves.

nodes.name: Base case $n = 0$
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the induction and check the constant case.

nodes.name: Decompose along the last variable
nodes.statement: Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \R^n \to \R$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \B^n$. We begin by decomposing \[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\] where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \B^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \B^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \B^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $p$ as a convex combination in $x_n$ of two bounded multilinear polynomials.

nodes.name: Apply the inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now for any $x \in \R^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have \begin{align*} |p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\ &\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\ &\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|) \end{align*} where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle inequality plus the inductive bound gives the product formula.

nodes.name: Behaviour of $p_\Rcal$ inside and outside $\P_\Rcal$
nodes.statement: There exists a function $a(x) = \exp\left(b_\Rcal\left(x\right)\cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$ such that for any $\Rcal \subseteq [R]$, the polynomial $p_\Rcal:[R]^N\to \R$ has degree $\tO(\sqrt{NT})$ and satisfies: \begin{align*} p_\Rcal(x) \in \begin{cases} [0,1/10] &\mathrm{if}~ x\in\P_\Rcal ~\mathrm{and}~ \SURJ_\Rcal(x)=0\\ [9/10,1] &\mathrm{if}~ x\in\P_\Rcal ~\mathrm{and}~ \SURJ_\Rcal(x)=1\\ [-a(x), a(x)]& \mathrm{if}~ x \notin \P_\Rcal.\end{cases} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $p_\Rcal$ has degree $\tO(\sqrt{NT})$, approximates $\SURJ_\Rcal$ on $\P_\Rcal$, and is at most $\exp(b_\Rcal(x)\tO(\sqrt T))$ elsewhere.
conclusions: There exists a function $a(x) = \exp\left(b_\Rcal\left(x\right)\cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$ such that the polynomial $p_\Rcal:[R]^N\to \R$ has degree $\tO(\sqrt{NT})$

nodes.name: Proof of the behaviour of $p_\Rcal$
nodes.statement: The first two cases are an immediate consequence of \Cref{approxlemma}. To upper bound the value of $|p_\Rcal(x)|$ for $x\notin \P_\Rcal$, we exploit the structure of $p_\Rcal$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\Rcal|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, $$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left(\id[x_1 = r], \dots, \id[x_N = r]\right).$$ If $b_\Rcal(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_\Rcal(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. However, by \Cref{lem:orT}, each of these $b_\Rcal(x)$ variables is still at most ${\exp(\tO(\sqrt{T}))}$. By \Cref{lem:real-bound}, \[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \Rcal} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_\Rcal(x) \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\] since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_\Rcal(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tO(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.
nodes.statement_short: The two bounded cases follow from the approximation lemma; outside $\P_\Rcal$ apply the multilinear growth bound to $w$ at the inflated inner values.

nodes.name: The two bounded cases
nodes.statement: The first two cases are an immediate consequence of \Cref{approxlemma}.
nodes.statement_short: Inside $\P_\Rcal$ the claim is the earlier approximation lemma.

nodes.name: Expose the inner variables $z_r$
nodes.statement: To upper bound the value of $|p_\Rcal(x)|$ for $x\notin \P_\Rcal$, we exploit the structure of $p_\Rcal$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\Rcal|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, $$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left(\id[x_1 = r], \dots, \id[x_N = r]\right).$$ If $b_\Rcal(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_\Rcal(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. However, by \Cref{lem:orT}, each of these $b_\Rcal(x)$ variables is still at most ${\exp(\tO(\sqrt{T}))}$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $b_\Rcal(x)$ inner values leave $[0,1]$, each at most $\exp(\tO(\sqrt T))$.

nodes.name: Apply the multilinear growth bound
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lem:real-bound}, \[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \Rcal} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_\Rcal(x) \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\] since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_\Rcal(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tO(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.
nodes.statement_short: The product bound collapses to the $b_\Rcal(x)$ bad factors.

nodes.name: Informal description of the polynomial approximation for $\SURJ$
nodes.statement: \State Sample $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ items and remove all range items seen from $[R]$. Let the remaining set be $\Rcal \subseteq [R]$. \State Solve $\SURJ_{\Rcal}$ under the promise that all $r\in\Rcal$ have $\fr_r(x)\leq T$, where $T=\tTheta(\sqrt{N})$.
nodes.statement_short: Sample $\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ items to discard frequent range items, then solve $\SURJ_\Rcal$ on the remaining low-frequency promise.

nodes.name: Sample and prune the range
nodes.statement: \State Sample $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ items and remove all range items seen from $[R]$. Let the remaining set be $\Rcal \subseteq [R]$.
nodes.statement_short: Discard range items witnessed in the sample; they are certainly present.

nodes.name: Solve the promise instance on the remaining items
nodes.statement: \State Solve $\SURJ_{\Rcal}$ under the promise that all $r\in\Rcal$ have $\fr_r(x)\leq T$, where $T=\tTheta(\sqrt{N})$.
nodes.statement_short: Run the hard-input polynomial $p_\Rcal$ on the surviving range items.

nodes.name: the sample-matching indicator $\id_y(x_\Scal)$
nodes.statement: To build up to this, consider a deterministic algorithm that queries a subset $\Scal \subseteq [N]$ of input elements, checks if the sampled string equals another fixed string $y$ and outputs $1$ if true and $0$ if false. If we denote the input $x\in[R]^N$ restricted to the subset $\Scal \subseteq [N]$ as $x_\Scal$, then this algorithm outputs $1$ if and only if $x_\Scal = y$. Interpreting the input as an element of $\B^{N \log R}$ rather than $[R]^N$, it is easy to see that a deterministic query algorithm querying $|\Scal|\log R$ bits of $x$ can solve this problem. Consequently, there is a polynomial of degree $|\Scal|\log R$ that outputs $1$ if $x_\Scal = y$ and outputs $0$ otherwise. For any fixed $\Scal \subseteq [N]$ and $y\in [R]^{|\Scal|}$, we denote this polynomial by $\id_y(x_\Scal)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\id_y(x_\Scal)$ is the degree-$|\Scal|\log R$ polynomial indicating that the sampled substring equals $y$.
differentia: outputs $1$ if $x_\Scal = y$ and outputs $0$ otherwise

nodes.name: Polynomial realizing sampling and hard-coded decisions
nodes.statement: Then the following polynomial samples a random set $\Scal$ of size $S$, reads the input $x$ restricted to the set $\Scal$, and outputs the bit $f(\Scal,x_\Scal)$: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} \id_y(x_\Scal) f(\Scal,y) \end{equation}

nodes.name: the residual range set $\Rcal(y)$
nodes.statement: Specifically, if we sample the set $\Scal \subseteq [N]$, and learn that $x_{\mathcal{S}}$ equals the string $y\in[R]^{|\Scal|}$, then we want to run the polynomial $p_\Rcal(y)$ from \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ} for the set $\Rcal(y)$ of all elements in $[R]$ that do not appear in $y$, i.e., \begin{equation} \Rcal(y) = [R] \setminus \{r:\exists i~y_i = r\}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the set of all elements in $[R]$ that do not appear in $y$

nodes.name: the final approximating polynomial $r(x)$ for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Using the tools from \Cref{sec:surj-hard-inputs} and the above discussion, we can now construct a polynomial that corresponds to the informal description in \Cref{alg:SURJalmost}: \begin{equation} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} \id_y(x_\Scal) p_{\Rcal(y)}(x). \end{equation} This is a polynomial of degree $S\log R + \max_{y}\{\deg(p_{\Rcal(y)})\} = \tO(S + \sqrt{NT}) = \tO(N^{3/4})$, using $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ and $T=\tTheta(\sqrt{N})$ (where the factors hidden by the $\tTheta$ notation will be chosen later).
nodes.statement_short: $r(x)$ averages $p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)$ over all samples $\Scal$ of size $S$ and has degree $\tO(N^{3/4})$.

nodes.name: Probability that $b$ frequent range items are missed by the sample
nodes.statement: Let $S, T \le N$. Let $\Scal \subset [N]$ be a random subset of size $S$. Then for every $x \in [R]^N$ and every $b \ge 1$, \[\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \ge b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot (ST/N - \log N))},\] recalling that $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}$ is the number of range items $r \in \Rcal$ that appear in $x$ more than $T$ times, but do not appear in $x_\Scal$.
nodes.statement_short: Missing $b$ of the frequent range items in a size-$S$ sample has probability $\exp(-b(ST/N - \log N))$.
assumptions: Let $\Scal \subset [N]$ be a random subset of size $S$

nodes.name: Proof of the sampling probability bound
nodes.statement_short: Bound the conditional miss probabilities by $\exp(-ST/N)$ each, multiply, and union bound over the at most $\binom{N/T}{b}$ choices of frequent items.

nodes.name: Analyze a simplified experiment
nodes.statement:
To calculate the probability of interest, we begin by analyzing a simplified experiment. Suppose there are $b$ range items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ each appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. We compute the probability that \emph{none} of the items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear in the sample $x_\Scal$. If $T \ge N - S$, then this probability is zero. Otherwise, by direct calculation, we have for each $i = 1, \dots, b$: \[\Pr_{\Scal}[r_i 
otin x_\Scal | r_1 
otin x_\Scal, \dots, r_{i-1} 
otin x_\Scal] \le \prod_{j = 0}^{S-1} \left(1 -  rac{T}{N-j} ight) \le \left( 1 -  rac{T}{N}ight)^S \le \exp \left(- rac{ST}{N} ight).\]
nodes.statement_short: Each frequent item is missed with conditional probability at most $\exp(-ST/N)$.

nodes.name: Multiply the conditional probabilities
nodes.statement:
Hence the probability that none of $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear is \[\Pr_{\Scal}[r_1 
otin x_\Scal \land \dots \land r_b 
otin x_\Scal] = \prod_{i = 1}^b \Pr_{\Scal}[r_i 
otin x_\Scal | r_1 
otin x_\Scal, \dots, r_{i-1} 
otin x_\Scal] \le \exp \left(- rac{bST}{N} ight).\]
nodes.statement_short: The chain rule gives $\exp(-bST/N)$ for missing all $b$ items.

nodes.name: Union bound over choices of frequent items
nodes.statement: Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$: \begin{align*} \Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\Scal}[r_{i_j} \notin x_\Scal \quad \forall j \in Y] \\ & \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\ &\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: At most $N/T$ items are frequent, so the union bound costs only $e^{b\log N}$.

nodes.name: Completion of the proof of the upper bound for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Recalling that $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}$ is the number of range items $r \in \Rcal$ that appear in $x$ greater than $T$ times (cf. Equation \eqref{eq:b}), we compute the value of the polynomial $r(x)$ on an input $x$: \begin{align} r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \right)\\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x), \end{align} where we split up the sum into the $b=0$ \eqref{eq:t1} and $b\geq 1$ \eqref{eq:t2} cases. We first show that the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} has essentially no contribution to the final value. When $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \geq 1$, we know by \Cref{lem:boundonprcal} that the magnitude of the polynomial $|p_\Rcal(x)|$ is at most $\exp\left(b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$. Thus the magnitude of the term in Expression \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} &\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot \exp(b \cdot \tO(\sqrt{T})) \\ =&\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot \exp\left(b \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right). \end{align} We now need to compute the value of $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b]$ for each $b$. Intuitively, this roughly corresponds to the probability that we sample $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ elements from the input and miss all $bT$ elements that correspond to the $T = \tTheta(\sqrt{N})$ copies of the $b$ range items that appear at least $T$ times. If we were to sample $N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of seeing none of the $b T$ elements would be $\Theta(1)$. Since we are sampling $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4}) \gg N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of not seeing one of the $bT$ elements is ${\exp(-bST/N)} = {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(N^{1/4}))}$. We make this heuristic calculation formal in the following lemma:
nodes.statement_short: Split the average over samples by the number $b$ of missed frequent items and bound the $b \ge 1$ tail via the growth bound on $p_\Rcal$.

nodes.name: Conclusion of the proof of the upper bound for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: From \Cref{lem:prob-b} we know that $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(ST/N))}$. Hence the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(ST/N))} \cdot {\exp(b \cdot \tO(\sqrt{T}))} = o(1), \end{align} by choosing $T = \tTheta(\sqrt{N})$ and $S = \tTheta(N^{3/4})$ appropriately. This shows that the term in \eqref{eq:t2} does not significantly influence the value of the polynomial for any input $x$. Thus we have for any input $x$, \begin{align} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) + o(1). \end{align} By \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ}, we know that if $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0$ (and hence $x \in \P_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}$), then $p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) $ is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\SURJ(x)$. Applying \Cref{lem:prob-b} once again shows that $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \ge 1] \le \exp(- \tOmega(N^{1/4}))$, so $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) = 0] = 1 - o(1)$. Hence, for all $x \in [R]^N$, $|r(x) - \SURJ(x)| \le 1/10 + o(1) \le 1/3$. This completes the proof of \Cref{thm:upper}.
nodes.statement_short: The $b \ge 1$ tail is $o(1)$ and, with probability $1-o(1)$, the $b=0$ term is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\SURJ$, so the total error is at most $1/3$.

nodes.name: Split the average by the number of missed frequent items
nodes.statement: Recalling that $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}$ is the number of range items $r \in \Rcal$ that appear in $x$ greater than $T$ times (cf. Equation \eqref{eq:b}), we compute the value of the polynomial $r(x)$ on an input $x$: \begin{align} r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \right)\\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x), \end{align} where we split up the sum into the $b=0$ \eqref{eq:t1} and $b\geq 1$ \eqref{eq:t2} cases.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $r(x)$ into the $b=0$ term and the $b\ge 1$ tail.

nodes.name: Bound the $b \ge 1$ tail by the growth bound
nodes.statement: We first show that the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} has essentially no contribution to the final value. When $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \geq 1$, we know by \Cref{lem:boundonprcal} that the magnitude of the polynomial $|p_\Rcal(x)|$ is at most $\exp\left(b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$. Thus the magnitude of the term in Expression \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} &\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot \exp(b \cdot \tO(\sqrt{T})) \\ =&\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \cdot \exp\left(b \cdot \tO\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Replace $|p_\Rcal|$ by its exponential growth bound and rewrite as a probability sum.

nodes.name: Estimate the probability of missing $b$ frequent items
nodes.statement: We now need to compute the value of $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b]$ for each $b$. Intuitively, this roughly corresponds to the probability that we sample $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$ elements from the input and miss all $bT$ elements that correspond to the $T = \tTheta(\sqrt{N})$ copies of the $b$ range items that appear at least $T$ times. If we were to sample $N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of seeing none of the $b T$ elements would be $\Theta(1)$. Since we are sampling $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4}) \gg N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of not seeing one of the $bT$ elements is ${\exp(-bST/N)} = {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(N^{1/4}))}$.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristically the miss probability is $\exp(-b\tOmega(N^{1/4}))$.

nodes.name: Conclude the $b \ge 1$ tail is $o(1)$
nodes.statement: From \Cref{lem:prob-b} we know that $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(ST/N))}$. Hence the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} {\exp(-b \cdot \tOmega(ST/N))} \cdot {\exp(b \cdot \tO(\sqrt{T}))} = o(1), \end{align} by choosing $T = \tTheta(\sqrt{N})$ and $S = \tTheta(N^{3/4})$ appropriately. This shows that the term in \eqref{eq:t2} does not significantly influence the value of the polynomial for any input $x$.
nodes.statement_short: The sampling bound beats the growth bound for $T=\tTheta(\sqrt N)$, $S=\tTheta(N^{3/4})$.

nodes.name: Conclude the $b = 0$ term approximates $\SURJ$
nodes.statement: Thus we have for any input $x$, \begin{align} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\Scal \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \id[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) + o(1). \end{align} By \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ}, we know that if $b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x)=0$ (and hence $x \in \P_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}$), then $p_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) $ is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\SURJ(x)$. Applying \Cref{lem:prob-b} once again shows that $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) \ge 1] \le \exp(- \tOmega(N^{1/4}))$, so $\Pr_{\Scal}[b_{\Rcal(x_\Scal)}(x) = 0] = 1 - o(1)$. Hence, for all $x \in [R]^N$, $|r(x) - \SURJ(x)| \le 1/10 + o(1) \le 1/3$. This completes the proof of \Cref{thm:upper}.
nodes.statement_short: With probability $1-o(1)$ no frequent item is missed, giving total error $\le 1/3$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the approximate degree of Surjectivity
nodes.statement: For some $N = O(R)$, the $(1/3)$-approximate degree of $\SURJ_{N, R}$ is $\tOmega(R^{3/4})$.

nodes.name: Hardness amplification for $\AND_R \circ \OR_N$ under the Hamming weight promise
nodes.statement: Let $N = c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c>0$. Let $F^{\le N} \colon H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} \to \bits$ equal $\AND_{R} \circ \OR_N$ restricted to inputs in $H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} = \{x \in \bits^{N \cdot R} : |x| \le N\}$. Then $\ubdeg(F^{\le N}) \ge \tOmega(R^{3/4}).$
assumptions: Let $N = c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c>0$
Let $F^{\le N} \colon H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} \to \bits$ equal $\AND_{R} \circ \OR_N$ restricted to inputs in $H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} = \{x \in \bits^{N \cdot R} : |x| \le N\}$

nodes.name: Three-step outline of the proof of the amplification theorem
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{thm:main-amp} entails using dual witnesses for the high approximate degree of $\AND_R$ and $\OR_N$ to construct a dual witness for the higher approximate degree of $F^{\le N}$. As indicated in \Cref{s:overview}, the construction is essentially the same as in~\cite{adegsurj}, except that we observe that a dual witness for $\OR$ constructed and used in prior works satisfies an exponentially stronger decay condition than has been previously realized. The construction can be thought of as consisting of three steps: \paragraph{Step 1.} We begin by constructing a dual witness $\psi$ for the fact that the unbounded approximate degree of the $\OR_N$ function is $\Omega\left(\sqrt{T}\right)$ even when promised that the input has Hamming weight at most $T = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$. The dual witness $\psi$ is a small variant of the one in~\cite{adegsurj}, but we give a more careful analysis of its tail decay. In particular, we make use of the fact that for all $t \ge 1$, the $\ell_1$ weight that $\psi$ places on the $t$'th layer of the Hamming cube is upper bounded by $\exp(-\Omega(t/\sqrt{T})) / t^2$. \paragraph{Step 2.} We combine $\psi$ with a dual witness $\Phi$ for $\AND_R$ to obtain a preliminary dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ for $F = \AND_R \circ \OR_N$. The dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ shows that $F$ has approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{R} \cdot \sqrt{T}) = \Omega(R^{3/4})$. However, $\Phi \ls \psi$ places weight on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, and hence does not give an \emph{unbounded} approximate degree lower bound for the promise variant $F^{\le N}$. \paragraph{Step 3.} Using \Cref{prop:btzeroing} we zero out the mass that $\Phi \ls \psi$ places on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, while maintaining its pure high degree and correlation with $F^{\le N}$. This yields the final desired \emph{unbounded} approximate degree dual witness $\zeta$ for $F^{\le N}$, as per \Cref{prop:ub-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Build a decaying dual witness for $\OR_N$, combine it with one for $\AND_R$ by dual block composition, then zero out the high-Hamming-weight mass.

nodes.name: Step 1: dual witness for $\OR_N$ with strong tail decay
nodes.statement: We begin by constructing a dual witness $\psi$ for the fact that the unbounded approximate degree of the $\OR_N$ function is $\Omega\left(\sqrt{T}\right)$ even when promised that the input has Hamming weight at most $T = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$. The dual witness $\psi$ is a small variant of the one in~\cite{adegsurj}, but we give a more careful analysis of its tail decay. In particular, we make use of the fact that for all $t \ge 1$, the $\ell_1$ weight that $\psi$ places on the $t$'th layer of the Hamming cube is upper bounded by $\exp(-\Omega(t/\sqrt{T})) / t^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\psi$ for $\OR_N$ and analyze its exponential layer decay.

nodes.name: Step 2: combine with a dual witness for $\AND_R$
nodes.statement: We combine $\psi$ with a dual witness $\Phi$ for $\AND_R$ to obtain a preliminary dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ for $F = \AND_R \circ \OR_N$. The dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ shows that $F$ has approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{R} \cdot \sqrt{T}) = \Omega(R^{3/4})$. However, $\Phi \ls \psi$ places weight on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, and hence does not give an \emph{unbounded} approximate degree lower bound for the promise variant $F^{\le N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Dual block composition yields an $\Omega(R^{3/4})$ witness that still charges heavy inputs.

nodes.name: Step 3: zero out the high Hamming weight mass
nodes.statement: Using \Cref{prop:btzeroing} we zero out the mass that $\Phi \ls \psi$ places on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, while maintaining its pure high degree and correlation with $F^{\le N}$. This yields the final desired \emph{unbounded} approximate degree dual witness $\zeta$ for $F^{\le N}$, as per \Cref{prop:ub-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the zeroing-out proposition to get the final unbounded-degree witness $\zeta$.

nodes.name: Univariate dual witness for $\OR$ with exponential tail decay
nodes.statement: Let $T \in \N$ and $1/T \le \delta \le 1/2$. There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1) $ and a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \R$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge 1- \delta \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^T |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \R \to \R\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T})}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N
nodes.statement_short: There is a unit-norm univariate dual witness for $\OR$ with pure high degree $c_1\sqrt{\delta T}$ whose weight decays exponentially in $t$.
conclusions: There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1)$ and a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \R$ such that $\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge 1- \delta$
For all univariate polynomials $q \colon \R \to \R$, $\deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0$

nodes.name: Combinatorial identity for alternating binomial sums
nodes.statement: Let $T \in \N$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then \[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\]
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N
nodes.origin_citation: Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics Eq. (5.23); O'Donnell and Servedio
assumptions: Let $T \in \N$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$

nodes.name: Proof of the univariate dual witness for $\OR$
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N
nodes.statement_short: Define $\omega$ from the Špalek-style product over a sparse set $S$ of quadratically spaced points, then verify pure high degree, layer-by-layer decay, and correlation.

nodes.name: Renormalize the goal
nodes.statement: By renormalizing, it suffices to construction a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \R$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge (1 - \delta)\|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \R \to \R\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} /\sqrt{T})\|\omega\|_1}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to constructing $\omega$ up to normalization by $\|\omega\|_1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N

nodes.name: Define the sparse set $S$ and the witness $\omega$
nodes.statement: Let $c = \lceil 8 / \delta \rceil$ below. We will freely use the fact that since $\delta \le 1/2$, we have $c \le c^2 / (c-1) \le 10 /\delta$. Let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/2c} \rfloor$ and define the set \[S = \{1, c\} \cup \{2ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| \ge c_1 \sqrt{\delta T}$ for some absolute constant $c_1 > 0$. Define the function \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]
nodes.statement_short: Support $\omega$ on quadratically spaced points via a signed binomial product.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N

nodes.name: Pure high degree via the combinatorial identity
nodes.statement: Property~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-phd-ref} follows from the following well-known combinatorial identity. \begin{fact}[e.g., \cite{concrete} Equation (5.23) or \cite{osnewbounds}] Let $T \in \N$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then \[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\] \end{fact} Expanding out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ reveals that \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S \setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Alternating binomial sums vanish, and $|\omega|$ has a closed product form on $S$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for OR_N

nodes.name: Decay at $t = 1$
nodes.statement: We now use this characterization to establish the improved tail decay property \eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}. This clearly holds for $t = 1$ with $c_2 = 1/10$, since $|\omega(1)| \le \|\omega\|_1$ and \[\frac{170}{\delta} \exp(-c_2\sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}) \ge 340 \cdot e^{-\sqrt{2} / 10} > 1.\]
nodes.statement_short: The claimed bound is trivial at $t=1$.

nodes.name: Decay at $t = c$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\omega(c)|/\omega(0)$ by $6/(c-1)$ and absorb the exponential factor.

nodes.name: Decay at the quadratic points $t = 2cj^2$
nodes.statement: For $t = 2cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} &= \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(2cj^2 - 1)(2cj^2-c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |2ci^2 - 2cj^2|} \\ &= \frac{c(m!)^2}{(4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} (i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} For $j \ge 1$, the first factor is bounded by \[\frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2},\] using the fact that $c \ge 2$. We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Since \[\frac{|\omega(t)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(2cj^2)|}{\omega(0)} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-2cj^2/(4cm)} \le \frac{170}{\delta \cdot t^2} \cdot e^{-t \sqrt{\delta} / 10 \sqrt{T}},\] this establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Split into a $1/t^2$ factorial factor and a factorial ratio bounded by $e^{-j^2/2m}$.

nodes.name: Dual polynomial for $\OR_N$ by Minsky-Papert symmetrization
nodes.statement: Let $T, N \in \N$ with $T \le N$, and let $\delta > 1/T$. Define $\omega$ as in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. Define the function $\psi: \bits^N \to \bits$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{ |x|}$ for $x \in H^N_{\le T}$ and $\psi(x) = 0$ otherwise. Then \begin{align} &\langle \psi, \OR_N \rangle \ge 1-\delta \\ & \|\psi\|_1 = 1 \\ & \text{For any polynomial } p \colon \bits^N \to \R\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \end{align}

nodes.name: Preliminary dual witness for $\AND_R \circ \OR_N$
nodes.statement: Let $\OR_N : \bits^N \to \bits$ \ and \ $\AND_R \colon \bits^R \to \bits$. \ Let $\psi\colon \bits^N \to \bits$ be a function such that $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$ and $\langle \psi, \OR_N \rangle \ge 19/20$. Then there exists a function $\Phi \colon \bits^R \to \bits$ with pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{R})$ and $\|\Phi\|_1 = 1$ such that \[ \langle \Phi \ls \psi, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle > 2/3.\]

nodes.name: Final dual witness for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be sufficiently large. There exist $N = O(R)$, $D = \tOmega(N^{3/4})$, and $\zeta : (\bits^N)^R \to \R$ such that \begin{align} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\sum_{x \in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}}\zeta(x) \cdot (\AND_{R} \circ \OR_N)(x) > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon (\bits^N)^R\to \R \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have } \langle p, \zeta \rangle = 0. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness
nodes.statement_short: There is a unit-norm dual witness for $\AND_R\circ\OR_N$ supported on Hamming weight $\le N$ with pure high degree $\tOmega(N^{3/4})$.
conclusions: There exist $N = O(R)$, $D = \tOmega(N^{3/4})$, and $\zeta : (\bits^N)^R \to \R$ such that $\zeta(x) = 0$ for all $x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}$
For every polynomial $p \colon (\bits^N)^R\to \R$ of degree less than $D$, we have $\langle p, \zeta \rangle = 0$

nodes.name: Proof of the final dual witness for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters: \begin{itemize} \item $d= \Theta(\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\AND_R$ in \Cref{prop:and-or}, \item $T = \lfloor(R/d)^{1/2}\rfloor^2 = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$, \item $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{T} \cdot d =\Theta(R^{3/4})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $\delta =1/20$ \item $\alpha = 170/\delta = 3400$, \item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T} = \Theta(1/R^{1/4})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = 693 R$. \end{itemize} Let $\psi : \bits^N \to \bits$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $\delta:=1/20$. Let $\Phi : \bits^R \to \bits$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:and-or}, and define $\xi = \Phi \ls \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align} Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tOmega(R^{3/4})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\bits^N)^R \to \R$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tOmega(R^{3/4})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:surj-dual}.

nodes.name: Apply the zeroing-out proposition
nodes.statement: Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tOmega(R^{3/4})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\bits^N)^R \to \R$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \AND_R \circ \OR_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Lower bound on the approximate degree of $k$-distinctness
nodes.statement: For $k \ge 2$ and some $N = O_k(R)$, the $(1/3)$-approximate degree of $\DIST^k_{N, R}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}_k(R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$. The same lower bound holds for the quantum query complexity of $\DIST^k_{N, R}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ under the Hamming weight promise
nodes.statement: Let $\promcomp : H_{\le N}^{N\cdot R} \to \bits$ equal $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ restricted to inputs in $H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}$. Then for some $N = O_k(R)$, we have $\ubdeg(\promcomp) \ge \tilde{\Omega}_k(R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$.
assumptions: Let $\promcomp : H_{\le N}^{N\cdot R} \to \bits$ equal $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ restricted to inputs in $H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}$

nodes.name: Three-step outline of the proof of the $k$-distinctness promise lower bound
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{thm:dist-promise} will follow the same basic outline as the proof of \Cref{thm:main-amp}. We will construct a dual polynomial for $\promcomp$ via the following three steps: \paragraph{Step 1.} We first construct a dual witness $\psi$ showing that the unbounded-approximate degree of the $\THR^k_N$ function is $\Omega_k\left(\sqrt{T N^{-1/k}}\right)$, even when promised that the input has Hamming weight at most $T = \Theta_k(\sqrt{R})$. Moreover, this dual witness satisfies additional properties that are exploited in Step 2 below. \paragraph{Step 2.} We combine $\psi$ with a dual witness $\Phi$ for $\OR_R$ to obtain a preliminary dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ for $\OR_R \circ \THR_N^k$. The dual witness $\Phi \ls \psi$ shows that $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ has approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{R} \cdot \sqrt{T}) = \Omega_k(R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$. However, $\Phi \ls \psi$ places weight on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, and hence does not give an \emph{unbounded} approximate degree lower bound for the promise variant $\promcomp$. \paragraph{Step 3.} Using \Cref{prop:btzeroing} we zero out the mass that $\Phi \ls \psi$ places on inputs of Hamming weight larger than $N$, while maintaining its pure high degree and correlation with $\promcomp$. This yields the final desired dual witness $\zeta$ for $\promcomp$.
nodes.statement_short: Same three-step template: a decaying dual witness for $\THR^k_N$, dual block composition with a witness for $\OR_R$, then zeroing out heavy inputs.

nodes.name: error regions $E_+(\psi, f)$ and $E_-(\psi, f)$
nodes.statement: For functions $f : \cX \to \bits$ and $\psi : \cX \to \mathbb{R}$, define the error regions \begin{align*} E_+(\psi, f) = \{x \in \cX : \psi(x) > 0, f(x) = -1\} \\ E_-(\psi, f) = \{x \in \cX : \psi(x) < 0, f(x) = +1\}. \end{align*} These are the regions where $\psi$ disagrees in sign with $f$. We refer to $E_+$ as the set of ``false positive'' errors made by $\psi$, and $E_-$ as the set of ``false negative'' errors.
nodes.genus: the regions where $\psi$ disagrees in sign with $f$

nodes.name: Univariate dual witness for $\THR^k_N$ with one-sided error control
nodes.statement: Let $k, T, N \in \N$ with $k \le T$. There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1] $ and a function $\omega : \{0, 1, \dots, T\} \to \R$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{\omega(t) > 0, t \ge k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48N} \\ & \sum_{\omega(t) < 0, t < k} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \\ & \|\omega\|_1 := \sum_{t = 0}^{T} |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \R \to \R\text{, } \notag \\ & \deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N
nodes.statement_short: There is a unit-norm univariate dual witness for $\THR^k_N$ with tiny false-positive mass, pure high degree $c_1\sqrt{T/(kN^{1/k})}$, and exponential decay.
conclusions: There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1]$ and a function $\omega : \{0, 1, \dots, T\} \to \R$ such that $\sum_{\omega(t) > 0, t \ge k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48N}$
For all univariate polynomials $q \colon \R \to \R$, $\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0$

nodes.name: Proof of the univariate dual witness for $\THR^k_N$
nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$. Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \R$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \R \to \R\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align} Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\] The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$. It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$. We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$. For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\] For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation} Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\] We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation} This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$. Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}. Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\omega$ supported on $\{1,\dots,k\}$ plus quadratically spaced points, then bound the head by binomials and the tail by $e^{-j^2/2m}$.

nodes.name: Dispose of the case $k = 1$
nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: The case $k=1$ is witnessed explicitly.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Normalize the goal and name the error sets
nodes.statement: Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \R$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \R \to \R\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Restate the targets relative to $\|\omega\|_1$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Define the support set $S$ and $\omega$
nodes.statement: Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\] The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$. It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Support $\omega$ on $\{1,\dots,k\}$ together with quadratically spaced points; sign it so $\omega(k)<0$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Decay for $t \le k$
nodes.statement: We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$.
nodes.statement_short: The bound is trivial on the head $t\le k$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Head and tail ratios to $|\omega(k)|$
nodes.statement: For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\] For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation} Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\] We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation} This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare every $|\omega(t)|$ to $|\omega(k)|$: binomials on the head, $e^{-j^2/2m}$ on the tail.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Bound the false-positive mass
nodes.statement: Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: All mass above $k$ is at most $|\omega(k)|/(48N)$, bounding $E_+$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N

nodes.name: Bound the false-negative mass
nodes.statement: Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Balancedness plus the mass concentration at $t=k$ gives the $1/2 - 2\cdot 4^{-k}$ bound.

nodes.name: Dual polynomial for $\THR^k_N$
nodes.statement: Let $k, T, N\in \N$ with $k \le T \le N$. Define $\psi : \bits^N \to \R$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{ |x|}$ for $x \in H_{\le T}^N$ and $\psi(x) = 0$ otherwise, where $\omega$ is as constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. Then \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, \THR^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, \THR^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k} \\ &\|\psi\|_1 = 1 \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \bits^N \to \R\text{, } \deg p < c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \\ &\sum_{|x| = t} |\psi(x)| \le (2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})/t^2 \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, N. \end{align}
nodes.section: 5.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for THR^k_N
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrizing $\omega$ over Hamming layers yields a dual witness for $\THR^k_N$ with the same error, degree, and decay guarantees.
assumptions: Let $k, T, N\in \N$ with $k \le T \le N$
Define $\psi : \bits^N \to \R$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{ |x|}$ for $x \in H_{\le T}^N$ and $\psi(x) = 0$ otherwise, where $\omega$ is as constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}

nodes.name: Roles of the error amplifier and the degree amplifier
nodes.statement: The dual witness $\Phi$ for $\OR_R$ that we construct will itself be obtained as a dual block composition $\rho \ls \varphi$. Each constituent dual polynomial will play a distinct role in showing that $\Phi \ls \psi$ is a good dual polynomial for $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$. The first function $\varphi$ is an ``error amplifier'' in the sense that $\varphi \ls \psi$ is much better correlated with $\OR_R \circ \THR^k_N$ than $\psi$ is with $\THR^k_N$. The second function $\rho$, on the other hand, is a ``degree amplifier'' in that it serves to increase the pure high degree of $\varphi \ls \psi$. While the amplification results we need are new, they are relatively straightforward extensions of similar results in~\cite{bt13, sherstovandor, bt14}. Proofs appear below for completeness.
nodes.section: 5.2 Step 2: A Preliminary Dual Witness for OR_R o THR^k_N
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi = \rho \ls \varphi$ splits into an error amplifier $\varphi$ and a degree amplifier $\rho$.

nodes.name: Amplifying error
nodes.statement: Let $f : \bits^m \to \bits$ and $\psi : \bits^m \to \R$ be functions such that \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^- \\ & \|\psi\|_1 = 1. \end{align} For every $M \in \N$, there exists a function $\varphi : \bits^M \to \bits$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \ls \psi, \OR_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \ls \psi)(x)| \le M \cdot \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \ls \psi, \OR_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \ls \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M. \end{align}
nodes.section: 5.2 Step 2: A Preliminary Dual Witness for OR_R o THR^k_N
nodes.statement_short: Composing with $\OR_M$ multiplies false positives by $M$ but drives false negatives down to $(2\delta^-)^M/2$.
assumptions: Let $f : \bits^m \to \bits$ and $\psi : \bits^m \to \R$ be functions such that $\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^+$
conclusions: there exists a function $\varphi : \bits^M \to \bits$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that $\sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \ls \psi, \OR_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \ls \psi)(x)| \le M \cdot \delta^+$

nodes.name: Proof of the error amplification proposition
nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi: \{-1, 1\}^M ightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ be defined such that $\varphi(\mathbf{1})=1/2$, $\varphi(-\mathbf{1})=-1/2$, and $\varphi(x)=0$ for all other $x$. Notice that  egin{equation} \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in \{-1, 1\}^M} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) = 0 \end{equation} so $\Psi$ has pure high degree $1$, and that $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$. We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$. Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \sgn(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$ when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. This allows us to write  egin{align} & \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^+(\varphi \ls \psi, \OR_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \ls \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| 
onumber \ & = 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \sgn(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathbb{I} (\varphi( \dots, \sgn(\psi(x_i)), \dots) > 0 \land \OR_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dotsight) = -1)] 
onumber\ & = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\OR_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \sgn(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \end{align} Observe that for any bit $b$, \[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) 
e \sgn(\psi(x)) | \sgn(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\] where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:  egin{itemize} \item The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on 
ewline $(\dots, \sgn(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$ \item The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. \end{itemize} Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals  egin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\OR_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \end{equation} where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$. By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$. Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have \[\Pr_y[\OR_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\] by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. It now remains to prove the bound~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-neg}. By an identical argument as above, we have  egin{equation}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^-(\varphi \ls \psi, \OR_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \ls \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) < 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\OR_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = 1]. \end{equation} The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\OR_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that \[\Pr_y[\OR_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dotsight) = 1] \le (2\delta^-)^M. \] It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.
